title: Early Islamic Egypt
subtitle: 641–969 · Fustat, the Caliphal Province, and the Dynasties of Ibn Tulun and the Ikhshid

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Egypt as a caliphal province governed from Fustat, then the autonomous dynasties of Ibn Tulun and the Ikhshid, to the Fatimid conquest

entries.label: The conquest generation and the naval province
entries.hint: For its first forty years Egypt was governed for the caliph — first from Medina, then from Umayyad Damascus — by 'Amr ibn al-'As and his successors, chief among them 'Abdallah ibn Sa'd. The Arab troops (the jund) were settled by tribe around the garrison town of Fustat and paid from the Egyptian tax revenue. The province's other role was naval: a war fleet built here beat the Byzantines at the Battle of the Masts in 655 and made Egypt the caliphate's western sea power.
entries.note: Al-Kindi, The Governors and Judges of Egypt (ed. Guest, 1912). Hugh Kennedy, 'Egypt as a Province in the Islamic Caliphate, 641–868', in Petry (ed.), The Cambridge History of Egypt, vol.1 (1998) pp.62–85.

entries.label: 'Abd al-Aziz ibn Marwan, the Marwanid viceroy
entries.hint: 'Abd al-Aziz, brother of the caliph 'Abd al-Malik, governed Egypt for twenty years almost as a hereditary viceroy, building at Hulwan south of Fustat (partly to escape recurrent plague), enlarging the mosque of 'Amr, and standing as heir apparent to the caliphate until he died a few months before his brother. His long, stable tenure entrenched Fustat as the seat of a self-contained provincial government.
entries.note: Al-Kindi, Governors and Judges. Petra Sijpesteijn, Shaping a Muslim State: The World of a Mid-Eighth-Century Egyptian Official (2013) pp.62–68; Kennedy in CHE1 (1998).

entries.label: Qurra ibn Sharik and the fiscal state
entries.hint: Under the governor Qurra ibn Sharik the Umayyad state pressed its demands on Egypt hard, and the papyri record it in detail: standing bilingual orders to the pagarch of the village of Aphrodito for tax silver, wheat, labourers for the caliphal fleet and for building at Jerusalem and Damascus, sailors, and the return of runaways. The Aphrodito archive of these years is the fullest picture anywhere of how the early caliphate actually governed a conquered province.
entries.note: The Aphrodito papyri: H.I. Bell, Greek Papyri in the British Museum IV: The Aphrodito Papyri (1910); the Arabic orders of Qurra, ed. Nabia Abbott (1938). Sijpesteijn, Shaping a Muslim State (2013).

entries.label: The fall of the Umayyads at Busir
entries.hint: The last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II, fled west across the Nile from the victorious Abbasid armies and was run down and killed at the village of Busir in Middle Egypt in August 750. The Abbasid revolution had reached Egypt; the province passed to governors appointed from the new capital in Iraq, and the focus of the caliphate moved decisively east, away from the Mediterranean.
entries.note: Al-Tabari, History, year 132; al-Kindi, Governors and Judges. Kennedy, The Early Abbasid Caliphate (1981).

entries.label: The Abbasid governors and al-Askar
entries.hint: Under the Abbasids Egypt was run by governors sent from Baghdad who rarely lasted more than a year or two, from a new administrative quarter, al-Askar, laid out beside Fustat. The tax burden rose, the Coptic countryside revolted repeatedly, and Arab tribal feuds convulsed the jund. Increasingly the caliph assigned Egypt's revenue to a courtier or general who never came, sending a deputy — a system that hollowed out central control.
entries.note: Al-Kindi, Governors and Judges. Kennedy in CHE1 (1998) pp.75–85; Wladimir Kubiak, Al-Fustat: Its Foundation and Early Urban Development (1987).

entries.label: The tax-farm and the Turkish generals
entries.hint: In the mid-ninth century, with the caliphate itself dominated by its Turkish soldiery at Samarra, Egypt was formally granted as a fiscal domain to figures at court — Turkish commanders like Bakbak and Yarjukh — who administered it through deputies. It was as the deputy of one such absentee governor that a young officer named Ahmad ibn Tulun arrived in Fustat in 868, at the head of a private following.
entries.note: Al-Kindi, Governors and Judges. Thierry Bianquis, 'Autonomous Egypt from Ibn Tulun to Kafur, 868–969', in Petry (ed.), The Cambridge History of Egypt, vol.1 (1998) pp.86–90.

entries.label: Ahmad ibn Tulun
entries.hint: Ahmad ibn Tulun, the son of a Turkish slave-soldier and himself raised at the Abbasid court, came to Egypt as a deputy governor and turned it into an independent state. He recruited his own army of Turks, Greeks and blacks, built a fleet, seized the tax administration, stopped forwarding the tribute to Baghdad, took Syria as far as the Byzantine frontier, and founded a royal city, al-Qata'i, north of Fustat, crowned by the great congregational mosque that still bears his name.
entries.note: Al-Balawi, Sirat Ahmad ibn Tulun; al-Kindi. Zaky M. Hassan, Les Tulunides (1933); Bianquis in CHE1 (1998) pp.90–99; Matthew Gordon, The Breaking of a Thousand Swords (2001) for the Turkish military context.

entries.label: Khumarawayh and the Tulunid collapse
entries.hint: Ahmad's son Khumarawayh won formal Abbasid recognition of Tulunid rule over Egypt and Syria and married his daughter to the caliph with a dowry that became a byword for extravagance — as did his gilded audience hall and his lake of quicksilver. He was murdered by his own slaves in Damascus in 896; the treasury he had drained could not sustain his young successors, and after a decade of factional chaos the dynasty was swept away.
entries.note: Al-Kindi; Ibn Sa'id. Bianquis in CHE1 (1998) pp.99–102; the marriage and dowry, al-Tabari, year 279.

entries.label: The Abbasid reconquest of 905
entries.hint: An Abbasid army and fleet under Muhammad ibn Sulayman al-Katib retook Egypt in 905; the Tulunid soldiery changed sides, and the royal city of al-Qata'i was plundered and demolished, only the mosque left standing. Thirty years of weak Abbasid governors followed, twice interrupted by failed Fatimid invasions from the west, until another autonomous Turkish soldier, Muhammad ibn Tughj, took control.
entries.note: Al-Kindi, Governors and Judges. Bianquis in CHE1 (1998) pp.102–06.

entries.label: Muhammad ibn Tughj al-Ikhshid
entries.hint: Muhammad ibn Tughj, of a Central Asian soldier family, made himself autonomous ruler of Egypt and obtained from the powerless caliph the old Farghana royal title 'al-Ikhshid'. He built the state on a strong army and a full treasury, held southern Syria and the holy cities of the Hijaz against both the Baghdad-backed Hamdanids and the rising Fatimids of North Africa, and passed a functioning, if fragile, state to his sons under a regent.
entries.note: Al-Kindi; Ibn Sa'id, al-Mughrib. Jere Bacharach, 'The Career of Muhammad ibn Tughj al-Ikhshid', Speculum 50 (1975); Bianquis in CHE1 (1998) pp.108–19.

entries.label: Kafur, the eunuch who ruled Egypt
entries.hint: Abu al-Misk Kafur, a black eunuch bought as a slave in his youth and given to al-Ikhshid, ran the Ikhshidid state for twenty-two years — first as regent and army commander for al-Ikhshid's young sons, then, from 966, as its recognised ruler, with his name in the Friday prayer. He kept Egypt intact against the Fatimids and the Qarmatians and drew poets to his court, including al-Mutanabbi, who left disappointed and immortalised him in savage verse.
entries.note: Al-Mutanabbi, Diwan (the Kafuriyyat). Ibn Khallikan, Wafayat al-A'yan. Bianquis in CHE1 (1998) pp.116–19; Nadia Maria El Cheikh and others on Kafur's image.

entries.label: The end of the Ikhshidids
entries.hint: Kafur's death left the eleven-year-old Ahmad ibn Ali nominally in charge, the court split between the vizier Ibn al-Furat and the Ikhshidid commanders, the treasury empty, and the Nile disastrously low, bringing famine and unrest. Fatimid agents moved through Fustat buying support and reassurance. When the Fatimid army appeared in 969, the Ikhshidid state had, in effect, already dissolved.
entries.note: Al-Maqrizi, Itti'az al-hunafa'; Ibn al-Athir. Michael Brett, The Rise of the Fatimids (2001) pp.295–314.

entries.label: Jawhar and the founding of Cairo
entries.hint: In July 969 the army of the Fatimid caliph al-Mu'izz, under the freedman general Jawhar al-Siqilli, entered Fustat almost without fighting on the strength of a written guarantee of safety. Jawhar at once laid out a new walled palace-city north of Fustat, al-Qahira ('the Victorious') — Cairo — and began its congregational mosque, al-Azhar. The Friday sermon was read in al-Mu'izz's name, and Egypt became the centre of a caliphate rivalling Baghdad.
entries.note: Al-Maqrizi, Itti'az al-hunafa' and Khitat. Michael Brett, The Rise of the Fatimids (2001) pp.295–314 and The Fatimid Empire (2017); Yaacov Lev, State and Society in Fatimid Egypt (1991).

entries.label: The Coptic patriarchate under Islam
entries.hint: The patriarch of Alexandria remained the head of Egypt's Christian majority and its official interlocutor with the Muslim state, increasingly resident near Fustat rather than in the old capital. His life could turn on the church's ability to pay its assessed taxes: patriarchs were fined, imprisoned and even (Khaʾil I, 750s) tortured over arrears. He also appointed the bishops of Christian Nubia and Ethiopia, extending Egyptian church authority up the Nile and into the Horn.
entries.note: The History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria, the Arabic recension begun by Severus ibn al-Muqaffa' in the 10th century. Maged Mikhail, From Byzantine to Islamic Egypt: Religion, Identity and Politics after the Arab Conquest (2014).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Umayyad-Abbasid war on the Nile, the Coptic tax revolts, the Tulunid and Abbasid reconquests, and the Fatimid arrival

entries.label: The Arab settlement and the naval war
entries.hint: After the conquest the Arab army was quartered by tribe around Fustat and paid from the land tax, while a Byzantine fleet still contested the sea. 'Abdallah ibn Sa'd built a war fleet in the Egyptian yards, and in 655 it broke the Byzantine navy under the emperor Constans II at the Battle of the Masts off the Lycian coast — the first major Arab victory at sea, and the event that secured Egypt against reconquest and made it the caliphate's Mediterranean naval base.
entries.note: Al-Tabari, year 34; Theophanes, Chronicle. Byzantine attempt on Alexandria (645): John of Nikiou. Walter Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992); Ekkehard Eickhoff, Seekrieg und Seepolitik zwischen Islam und Abendland (1966).

entries.label: The death of Marwan II at Busir
entries.hint: The last Umayyad caliph, defeated in Iraq and Syria, retreated across Egypt hoping to reach the Maghrib, burning bridges and boats behind him. An Abbasid column under Salih ibn Ali and 'Amir ibn Isma'il caught him near the village of Busir; he was killed in a night skirmish in the churchyard, and his head sent to the new caliph. Egypt passed to the Abbasids, and Umayyad and Alid loyalists were hunted through the province for years afterward.
entries.note: Al-Tabari, year 132; al-Kindi, Governors and Judges. Kennedy, The Early Abbasid Caliphate (1981) pp.42–45.

entries.label: The Coptic tax revolts and the Bashmuric war
entries.hint: For a century the Coptic peasantry rose against rising land tax, the extension of the poll tax to monks and the young, and abusive collection — in 725, 739, 750, 767 and repeatedly after. The largest rising, in the marsh country of Bashmur in the northeastern Delta in 831, held out long enough that the caliph al-Ma'mun came to Egypt in person; the general al-Afshin crushed it, deported the survivors and sold their families, and Coptic collective resistance was broken for good.
entries.note: The History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria; al-Kindi; al-Maqrizi, Khitat. Maged Mikhail, From Byzantine to Islamic Egypt (2014) pp.221–43; Kosei Morimoto, The Fiscal Administration of Egypt in the Early Islamic Period (1981).

entries.label: The Qays–Yaman feuds of the jund
entries.hint: The Arab settlers of Egypt were split, like the wider caliphate, between 'northern' (Qays/Mudar) and 'southern' (Yaman) tribal blocs, and the rivalry repeatedly turned violent — pitched fighting in Fustat and among the Delta garrison villages, governors made and unmade by one faction or the other, and Abbasid armies sent to impose order. The feuding was a chronic source of the province's instability and of its drift out of Baghdad's control.
entries.note: Al-Kindi, Governors and Judges, passim. Kennedy in CHE1 (1998) pp.70–75; the settlement geography in Sijpesteijn, Shaping a Muslim State (2013).

entries.label: Ibn Tulun's Syrian wars
entries.hint: Ahmad ibn Tulun extended his state into Syria in 877–878, taking Damascus, Homs, Aleppo and Antioch and reaching the Byzantine frontier at Tarsus, where the local garrison rebuffed him. He then faced down the Abbasid regent al-Muwaffaq, who declared him an outlaw, and put down a revolt by his own son al-Abbas. The wars gave Egypt a Syrian glacis and a battle-hardened army, both of which its successors fought to keep.
entries.note: Al-Balawi, Sirat Ahmad ibn Tulun; al-Tabari. Zaky M. Hassan, Les Tulunides (1933); Bianquis in CHE1 (1998) pp.94–99.

entries.label: The reconquest of 905
entries.hint: The Abbasid commander Muhammad ibn Sulayman advanced on Egypt by land and sea in 904–905. The Tulunid army, unpaid and demoralised after years of decline, largely defected; Fustat fell with little fighting; and the royal city of al-Qata'i was systematically plundered and pulled down, its palaces, hippodrome and gardens erased, leaving only Ibn Tulun's mosque standing alone on the desert edge.
entries.note: Al-Kindi, Governors and Judges; al-Maqrizi, Khitat (on al-Qata'i's destruction). Bianquis in CHE1 (1998) pp.101–02.

entries.label: The failed Fatimid invasions and the Syrian wars
entries.hint: The Fatimids of North Africa tried twice to take Egypt, in 914–915 and 919–921, landing in the west and reaching the Faiyum before Abbasid armies and fleets under Mu'nis al-Muzaffar drove them back. The Ikhshidids meanwhile fought the Hamdanids of Aleppo up and down Syria and warded off Qarmatian raids from the Arabian desert. For half a century Egypt's rulers held the country as a fortress between rival powers to east and west.
entries.note: Al-Tabari; Ibn al-Athir; al-Maqrizi, Itti'az. Yaacov Lev, 'The Fatimids and Egypt 301–358/914–969', Studia Islamica 66 (1987); Bianquis in CHE1 (1998).

entries.label: The Fatimid conquest and the Qarmatian aftermath
entries.hint: Jawhar's army entered a leaderless, famine-struck Egypt in 969 under a formal guarantee of safety to the people of Fustat, and met only a brief stand at the Nile crossing. The harder fight came after: Qarmatian armies from Syria, backed by Ikhshidid remnants, invaded twice, in 971 and 974, reaching the walls of the new city of Cairo before Jawhar and then the caliph al-Mu'izz himself beat them off, securing the Fatimid hold on Egypt.
entries.note: Al-Maqrizi, Itti'az al-hunafa'; Ibn al-Qalanisi. Michael Brett, The Rise of the Fatimids (2001) pp.295–345; Yaacov Lev, 'The Fatimid Conquest of Egypt', Journal of Semitic Studies 33 (1988).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The kharaj tax state, the Arabicisation of the chancery, the dhimma, and the garrison city as capital

entries.label: Fustat, the garrison city as capital
entries.hint: 'Amr's army built its permanent camp beside the fortress of Babylon rather than move into Alexandria, and it grew into Fustat, the seat of government for the next three centuries. Land was allotted in tribal blocks (khittas) around the mosque of 'Amr and the governor's residence; the army pay-register (diwan) organised the settlers; and Alexandria, the Greco-Roman metropolis, became a provincial port. Egypt's centre of gravity moved from the sea back to the head of the Delta, where Cairo stands today.
entries.note: Wladimir Kubiak, Al-Fustat: Its Foundation and Early Urban Development (1987); al-Maqrizi, Khitat. Petra Sijpesteijn, Shaping a Muslim State (2013) pp.68–80.

entries.label: The kharaj and jizya settlement
entries.hint: The conquest treaty set the basic fiscal order: a land tax (kharaj), assessed by survey and adjusted to the height of the flood, on all agricultural land; and a graduated poll tax (jizya) on adult non-Muslim men. Villages were collectively liable. This revenue — the reason Egypt had been worth conquering — funded the Arab garrison, was forwarded in large part to the caliphal centre, and shaped every relationship between the state and the Egyptian countryside.
entries.note: Kosei Morimoto, The Fiscal Administration of Egypt in the Early Islamic Period (1981); Gladys Frantz-Murphy, Arabic Agricultural Leases and Tax Receipts from Egypt (2001). The conquest terms: John of Nikiou; al-Baladhuri.

entries.label: The Christian scribes and their replacement
entries.hint: For two generations the Arab governors ran Egypt through the fiscal machinery they had inherited, staffed by the same Coptic and Greek Christian scribal families — pagarchs, financial officers, village clerks. The Aphrodito papyri show a Christian district administrator, Basileios, handling the Umayyad state's demands in Greek and Coptic. Then, as the registers were switched to Arabic and Muslims took the senior posts, this Christian administrative class was steadily displaced from the top of the system, though it lingered lower down for centuries.
entries.note: The Basileios/Aphrodito archive: Bell (1910); Sijpesteijn, Shaping a Muslim State (2013) — a study built around one such official. Maged Mikhail, From Byzantine to Islamic Egypt (2014).

entries.label: The Arabicisation of the state
entries.hint: Around the turn of the eighth century the caliph 'Abd al-Malik and his governors ordered the tax registers of Egypt kept in Arabic rather than Greek, introduced an Arabic-only coinage in place of the Byzantine-style types, and standardised Arabic protocol formulae on official papyrus. Within two generations the working language of the Egyptian state had changed from Greek and Coptic to Arabic — the first decisive step in a linguistic transformation that would take centuries to complete in the villages.
entries.note: Al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan (the register-language change); the coin sequence, Jere Bacharach, Islamic History through Coins (2006). The bilingual and then Arabic protocols: the Vienna and other papyrus collections.

entries.label: The dhimma in practice
entries.hint: Non-Muslims — the great majority of Egyptians for most of this period — held a protected but subordinate status: security of life, property and worship, and communal self-government under their own religious leaders, in return for the poll tax and acceptance of restrictions that hardened over time (distinguishing dress, limits on new churches, exclusion from some offices). In practice the rules were applied unevenly; Christians and Jews served as senior officials and physicians, and the papyri show mostly ordinary coexistence punctuated by episodes of pressure.
entries.note: The 'Pact of 'Umar' tradition: Mark Cohen, Under Crescent and Cross (1994). Egyptian practice: Tamer el-Leithy, and the documentary studies of Petra Sijpesteijn; Milka Levy-Rubin, Non-Muslims in the Early Islamic Empire (2011).

entries.label: The qadi and Islamic law in Egypt
entries.hint: Justice among Muslims passed from the governor's ad hoc rulings to a professional judge, the qadi of Fustat, sitting in the mosque of 'Amr and applying a body of law that was still taking shape. Egypt produced its own great jurist, al-Layth ibn Sa'd (d. 791), whom Malik of Medina rated his equal, though al-Layth's school did not outlast him. The judges' careers and rulings were later catalogued by al-Kindi, one of the first works of Islamic institutional history.
entries.note: Al-Kindi, The Governors and Judges of Egypt (Kitab al-Wulat wa-Kitab al-Qudat). Mathieu Tillier, Les cadis d'Iraq et l'État abbasside (2009) for method; on al-Layth, the biographical dictionaries.

entries.label: The apparatus of an autonomous state
entries.hint: Under Ibn Tulun and the Ikhshidids Egypt was governed as a state, not milked as a province. It kept a large standing paid army and a war fleet, a full treasury, a chancery, the royal textile administration, and — new for Egypt — public works on its own account: Ibn Tulun's hospital (872), one of the earliest in the Islamic world, offering free treatment; an aqueduct bringing water to al-Qata'i; markets, a hippodrome, a mint. The Fatimids inherited a working machine.
entries.note: Al-Balawi, Sirat Ahmad ibn Tulun; al-Maqrizi, Khitat. Bianquis in CHE1 (1998) pp.90–102; on the hospital, Ahmed Ragab, The Medieval Islamic Hospital (2015).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: A still-Christian country under Muslim rule — the Coptic patriarchate, al-Shafiʿi and Egyptian Islamic law, and the Jewish communities

entries.label: A still-Christian country
entries.hint: For most of this folio Egypt remained a Christian country under Muslim rule: the Coptic majority kept its churches, monasteries, festivals and pilgrimages, and its patriarch as communal head. Conversion to Islam was slow at first, driven less by preaching than by the poll tax, the ceiling on Christian careers, and the shocks of the tax revolts and their repression. Only from the ninth and tenth centuries did the balance begin to shift, and Egypt would not become majority-Muslim for generations more.
entries.note: Richard Bulliet, Conversion to Islam in the Medieval Period (1979) for the disputed timing. Maged Mikhail, From Byzantine to Islamic Egypt (2014); Tamer el-Leithy, 'Coptic Culture and Conversion in Medieval Cairo' (2005).

entries.label: al-Shafiʿi and the making of Egyptian Islamic law
entries.hint: Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafiʿi came to Fustat in 814, taught in the mosque of 'Amr, revised his legal theory into the 'new' teaching, and dictated the Risala on the sources of law and the vast Umm before dying there in 820. His system — placing the Prophet's example, transmitted as hadith, at the centre of jurisprudence — became one of the four Sunni schools and the dominant one in Egypt. His tomb in the Qarafa cemetery grew into the greatest Muslim shrine in the country.
entries.note: Al-Shafiʿi, al-Risala (Majid Khadduri's translation, 1961) and Kitab al-Umm. Joseph Lowry, Early Islamic Legal Theory: The Risala of Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafiʿi (2007); the tomb, later monumentalised by the Ayyubids.

entries.label: The mosque of 'Amr and Muslim Fustat
entries.hint: The mosque 'Amr's men built in 642, the first in Africa, was rebuilt and enlarged again and again as Fustat grew, and served as the city's Friday mosque, its main court of law, and a centre of teaching where jurists like al-Shafiʿi held circles. Around it a Muslim urban society took shape — quarters, markets, a governing and scholarly class — alongside, and gradually overtaking, the Christian and Jewish city.
entries.note: Al-Maqrizi, Khitat, on the mosque's successive enlargements. K.A.C. Creswell, Early Muslim Architecture (1932–40) vol.1. Kubiak, Al-Fustat (1987).

entries.label: Dhu al-Nun and the beginnings of Egyptian Sufism
entries.hint: Dhu al-Nun al-Misri, a scholar of Nubian descent from Akhmim in Upper Egypt, is remembered as one of the founders of the Sufi tradition: he is credited with introducing the systematic teaching of the mystical 'states' and 'stations' and a doctrine of intimate, ecstatic knowledge (maʿrifa) of God, and was tried for heresy in Baghdad before being released. His example, and the older Christian ascetic landscape of Egypt around him, seeded a distinctively Egyptian strand of Islamic mysticism and saint-veneration.
entries.note: The Sufi biographical tradition: al-Sulami, Tabaqat al-Sufiyya; al-Qushayri, Risala. Michael Ebstein and others on Dhu al-Nun; the hermetic-alchemical texts attributed to him.

entries.label: The Jewish communities of Fustat
entries.hint: Fustat and Alexandria held substantial Jewish communities, self-governing under the dhimma. The Rabbanites of Fustat were split into two congregations, one following the customs of the Iraqi academies and one those of Palestine — the latter worshipping in the synagogue later called Ben Ezra, whose storeroom would preserve the Cairo Geniza. From the ninth century a Karaite community, rejecting rabbinic tradition for scripture alone, grew alongside them. The heads of the Jewish world in Iraq and Palestine both claimed Egyptian allegiance.
entries.note: S.D. Goitein, A Mediterranean Society (1967–93) — largely on the Fatimid-and-later Geniza, but with the earlier background. Marina Rustow, Heresy and the Politics of Community: The Jews of the Fatimid Caliphate (2008).

entries.label: The monasteries endure and thin
entries.hint: The monastic centres — Scetis in the Wadi Natrun, the White Monastery, the desert houses of Upper Egypt — kept working through the early Islamic centuries, producing and copying the theological, liturgical and hagiographical literature of the Coptic church and drawing pilgrims. But they were squeezed: the poll tax was extended to monks, Bedouin raids sacked Scetis repeatedly (817, 866), and numbers fell. The monasteries became the shrinking reservoir of Coptic learning and identity.
entries.note: Hugh Evelyn White, The Monasteries of the Wâdi 'n Natrûn (1926–33). The History of the Patriarchs on the raids; Ewa Wipszycka, The Second Gift of the Nile: Monks and Monasteries in Late Antique Egypt (2018) for the earlier picture.

entries.label: Egypt and the churches of Nubia and Ethiopia
entries.hint: The Coptic patriarch of Alexandria was the head of a Nile-wide Christian world at its height. He consecrated the bishops of the three Christian kingdoms of Nubia and appointed the single metropolitan (abun) of the Ethiopian church, a monk sent from Egypt. The baqt treaty with Nubia contained provisions for the churches; Nubian clergy and pilgrims came to Fustat; and when a caliph or governor pressed the Egyptian church too hard, the Nubian king could send an army north in protest.
entries.note: The History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria; Giovanni Vantini, Oriental Sources concerning Nubia (1975). Derek Welsby, The Medieval Kingdoms of Nubia (2002); on Ethiopia, Steven Kaplan and the abun tradition.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Mosque of Ibn Tulun, the tiraz textiles, Fustat lustre pottery, and Coptic-Arabic literature

entries.label: The Mosque of Ibn Tulun
entries.hint: Ahmad ibn Tulun crowned his new royal city with a congregational mosque built of brick on a scale nothing in Egypt matched — a vast arcaded courtyard, pointed arches carried on piers, carved stucco friezes running the length of the sanctuary, and a spiralling external minaret copied from the caliphal capital of Samarra. When al-Qata'i was demolished after 905 the mosque alone was spared, and it survives essentially intact — the one great monument of the whole early Islamic period in Egypt.
entries.note: K.A.C. Creswell, Early Muslim Architecture (1932–40) vol.2; Doris Behrens-Abouseif, Islamic Architecture in Cairo (1989) pp.51–57. Al-Balawi, Sirat Ahmad ibn Tulun.

entries.label: The tiraz workshops
entries.hint: The state ran royal textile factories — the dar al-tiraz — chiefly in the Delta towns of Tinnis and Damietta, which wove fine linen and linen-and-silk shot through with bands of inscription naming the reigning ruler, the workshop and the year, along with Qurʾanic and pious phrases. The finished cloth was cut into robes of honour for officials and envoys and sold across the Mediterranean world. Thousands of dated fragments survive, and Egypt's Delta linen was as prized in this period as at any time in its history.
entries.note: R.B. Serjeant, Islamic Textiles: Material for a History up to the Mongol Conquest (1972). The tiraz inscriptions: the corpora of Adolf Grohmann and Étienne Combe; Yedida Stillman, Arab Dress (2000).

entries.label: Fustat lustreware and the potters' quarter
entries.hint: The kilns of Fustat made it one of the great ceramic centres of the medieval world. Its potters took up tin-opacified white glaze and, from the ninth century, lustre painting — a shimmering metallic film fired over the glaze in a reducing kiln — imitating the effect of precious metal, and produced blue-splashed and incised wares imitating imported Chinese stoneware. The mountains of wasters in the Fustat rubbish mounds, and finds of Egyptian lustre as far as Italy, mark the scale of the trade.
entries.note: Aly Bahgat & Félix Massoul, La céramique musulmane de l'Égypte (1930); George Scanlon's Fustat excavation reports (ARCE, 1960s–70s); Marilyn Jenkins-Madina, Raqqa Revisited (2006) for the lustre debate.

entries.label: Coptic Christianity writes in Arabic
entries.hint: By the tenth century the Coptic church needed to think and argue in Arabic. Severus ibn al-Muqaffa', bishop of al-Ashmunayn, wrote Arabic treatises defending Christian doctrine against Muslim and Jewish objections and, above all, launched the History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria in Arabic. Bible translations, saints' lives and theology followed the same path. Coptic was becoming a liturgical language only, while the community's living literature moved into the language of its rulers.
entries.note: Severus ibn al-Muqaffa', Refinement of the Understanding (Tartib al-Kahanut) and the polemical works; Samir Khalil Samir on the Christian Arabic corpus. Sidney Griffith, The Church in the Shadow of the Mosque (2008).
keywords: History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria

entries.label: Late Coptic art and the new vocabulary
entries.hint: The late-antique Coptic visual tradition carried on and slowly changed under Islam: tapestry-woven textiles, carved wood and bone, illuminated Gospel books, and the painted programmes of the surviving monastery churches — the layered figures of Christ, the Virgin and ranks of saints in the Red Monastery near Sohag are among the finest. Over time the decorative repertoire absorbed Islamic geometric and vegetal motifs, and the two artistic worlds of Egypt began to converge.
entries.note: Elizabeth Bolman (ed.), The Red Monastery Church: Beauty and Asceticism in Upper Egypt (2016). Coptic wood and ivory: the Coptic Museum, Cairo collections; Gawdat Gabra & Marianne Eaton-Krauss, The Illustrated Guide to the Coptic Museum (2007).

entries.label: al-Mutanabbi at the court of Kafur
entries.hint: The greatest of Arabic poets, Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi, spent four years at Kafur's court in Fustat, writing panegyrics in hope of a governorship. When it did not come he slipped away and turned his gift against his patron in some of the most famous invective in the language — mocking a black eunuch slave for ruling Egypt. The episode fixed both men in literary memory and marks the height of Arabic court poetry on the Nile before the Fatimids.
entries.note: Al-Mutanabbi, Diwan, the Kafuriyyat cycle. Régis Blachère, Un poète arabe du IVe siècle de l'Hégire: Abou t-Tayyib al-Motanabbi (1935); A.J. Arberry, Poems of al-Mutanabbi (1967).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Egyptian jurisprudence, the History of the Patriarchs, the Nilometer of Roda, and the transmission of learning

entries.label: The History of the Patriarchs
entries.hint: Severus ibn al-Muqaffa' and his collaborators gathered the Coptic, Greek and oral records of the bishops of Alexandria from St Mark onward and cast them as a continuous Arabic chronicle, the History of the Patriarchs — thereafter kept up, patriarch by patriarch, for a thousand years. It is the indispensable narrative source for Christian Egypt across the whole medieval period and a founding work of Middle Eastern communal history.
entries.note: History of the Patriarchs of the Coptic Church of Alexandria: B. Evetts (ed. & tr.), Patrologia Orientalis 1, 5, 10 (1907–15); the continuations ed. Aziz Atiya and others. Johannes den Heijer, Mawhub ibn Mansur ibn Mufarrig et l'historiographie copto-arabe (1989).

entries.label: al-Kindi and the history of a province
entries.hint: Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Kindi wrote a paired history of the governors and of the judges of Egypt from the conquest to his own day — a systematic, office-by-office record of how the province had actually been administered and judged. It began a strong Egyptian tradition of local and institutional history, distinct from the caliphal chronicles of Iraq, that runs through Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam and al-Musabbihi to the great topographer al-Maqrizi five centuries later.
entries.note: Al-Kindi, Kitab al-Wulat wa-Kitab al-Qudat (ed. Rhuvon Guest, 1912). Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr (the earlier conquest narrative). Tarif Khalidi, Arabic Historical Thought in the Classical Period (1994).

entries.label: The Nilometer of Roda
entries.hint: The state's single most important scientific instrument was rebuilt on the southern tip of Roda island opposite Fustat in 861, under the caliph al-Mutawakkil: an octagonal marble column standing in a stone-lined pit connected to the river, graduated in cubits and fingers. Officials read the daily rise, and once the water reached the mark that meant a full irrigation — the 'sultan's cubit' — the tax became due and the criers announced 'the Nile is complete'. It still stands, one of the oldest Islamic buildings in Egypt.
entries.note: K.A.C. Creswell, Early Muslim Architecture, vol.2; William Popper, The Cairo Nilometer (1951). The engineers: the tradition names Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Hasib and associates of al-Farghani.

entries.label: Alchemy, medicine and the transmitted sciences
entries.hint: Egypt in this period was a consumer and passer-on of the sciences rather than a great centre of them. Books from the Baghdad translation movement circulated; medicine was practised at the mosque circles and, from 872, at Ibn Tulun's hospital, often by Christian and Jewish physicians attached to the courts; and a body of alchemical writing — some of it attached to the name of the mystic Dhu al-Nun — drew on the old Greco-Egyptian craft tradition. The Fatimid capital would soon change Egypt's scientific standing.
entries.note: On Dhu al-Nun and alchemy: Julius Ruska, and Michael Ebstein's work. Medicine and the hospital: Ahmed Ragab, The Medieval Islamic Hospital (2015). The wider setting: Dimitri Gutas, Greek Thought, Arabic Culture (1998).

entries.label: Coptic scholarship as a language dies
entries.hint: As spoken Coptic gave way to Arabic, the monasteries worked to preserve the written tradition: copying the Bible, the fathers and the saints' lives; compiling the Synaxarium, the church's daily calendar of commemorations; and producing the first Coptic–Arabic wordlists (sullam) and grammatical primers (muqaddima) so that clergy could still read the liturgy. It was scholarship in the service of a language sliding out of everyday use.
entries.note: Coptic grammars and scalae: Adel Sidarus, 'Coptic Lexicography in the Middle Ages', in Wilson (ed.), The Future of Coptic Studies (1978). The Wadi Natrun scriptoria: Evelyn White, The Monasteries of the Wâdi 'n Natrûn (1926–33).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The kharaj on the flood, the tiraz workshops, the Fustat crafts, and the Red Sea and Mediterranean trade

entries.label: The kharaj on the flood
entries.hint: The engine of the whole system was the land tax. Each year officials surveyed the cultivated area, rated it against the height the flood had reached, collected in cash and grain into district granaries, and forwarded the great bulk of it to the caliphal centre — Medina, then Damascus, then Baghdad. Egypt was among the richest of all the provinces, and its remittances were a major line of every early caliphal budget; the pressure to maximise them drove the Coptic revolts.
entries.note: Kosei Morimoto, The Fiscal Administration of Egypt in the Early Islamic Period (1981); Gladys Frantz-Murphy, The Agrarian Administration of Egypt from the Arabs to the Ottomans (1986). The remittance figures: al-Ya'qubi, al-Buldan.

entries.label: From tribute to tax-farm to assignment
entries.hint: The way the land revenue was raised drifted steadily away from the state. A fixed conquest tribute gave way to a directly assessed and collected kharaj; that in turn was increasingly let out to tax-farmers who paid a lump sum and kept what they could squeeze; and the revenue of whole districts was assigned to soldiers and courtiers (the qati'a, forerunner of the iqta') in place of a salary. Each step put more of Egypt's surplus into private hands and loosened the centre's grip.
entries.note: Frantz-Murphy, The Agrarian Administration of Egypt (1986) and Arabic Agricultural Leases and Tax Receipts from Egypt (2001). Claude Cahen, 'L'évolution de l'iqta' du IXe au XIIIe siècle', Annales ESC (1953).

entries.label: Linen and the textile economy
entries.hint: Flax was Egypt's great cash crop and linen its great manufacture. The Delta towns — Tinnis, Damietta, Shata, Dabiq — produced fine linen and linen-silk of a quality famous across the Islamic world and Byzantium, in state and private workshops, and shipped it out through Alexandria and the eastern ports. The industry employed a large part of the northern Delta and generated a stream of tax and export revenue that made the marshy Delta lakeside towns some of the wealthiest in Egypt.
entries.note: R.B. Serjeant, Islamic Textiles (1972). Tinnis: al-Muqaddasi, Ahsan al-Taqasim; the archaeological survey work of the Tinnis project (Alison Gascoigne).

entries.label: The crafts of Fustat
entries.hint: Fustat was a manufacturing city as much as a capital: potters and glassmakers whose kilns fed a Mediterranean trade, rock-crystal and metal workers, leather and paper (arriving from the east in this period), soap and sugar refining, and a dense network of workshops and markets. The excavated rubbish mounds — metres deep in kiln waste, broken glass, papyrus and cloth — and the later Geniza records together give an unusually complete picture of a medieval urban economy.
entries.note: George Scanlon's Fustat excavation reports (ARCE); Roland-Pierre Gayraud's Istabl 'Antar excavations. The material culture: Marilyn Jenkins, and the Benaki and Islamic Art Museum collections.

entries.label: The shrinking cultivated land
entries.hint: The area under cultivation contracted from its Roman peak. The desert-edge fields and Western-oasis agriculture that late antiquity had watered were largely given up, the Faiyum's irrigated zone pulled back, and farming concentrated on the reliably flooded central floodplain. Population decline from plague, the disruption of the revolts, and the neglect of marginal irrigation works all played a part; Egypt fed itself and exported grain, but from a smaller base than before.
entries.note: Alan Bowman & Eugene Rogan (eds.), Agriculture in Egypt from Pharaonic to Modern Times (1999). Faiyum contraction: the survey evidence and the tax-district lists; Frantz-Murphy, The Agrarian Administration of Egypt (1986).

entries.label: The coinage of the province and the dynasties
entries.hint: Egypt's coinage tracked its political status. After 697 the Byzantine-style gold gave way to purely epigraphic Islamic dinars and dirhams struck at Fustat in the caliph's name. When Ibn Tulun and then the Ikhshid and Kafur put their own names on the gold alongside the caliph's, it was a public statement of autonomy; and the debasement and shortage of silver in the last Ikhshidid years was a visible symptom of the fiscal collapse the Fatimids walked into.
entries.note: Jere Bacharach, Islamic History through Coins: An Analysis and Catalogue of Tenth-Century Ikhshidid Coinage (2006). The transition: the sylloge of Egyptian mint issues; Michael Bates on the reform coinage.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The Nilometer, the congregational mosque, textile and glass manufacture, and the war fleet

entries.label: The flood-and-tax hydraulic system
entries.hint: Islamic Egypt maintained the ancient basin-irrigation regime — the network of dyked flood basins, feeder canals and regulators that spread and held the inundation across the fields — under a new administration, with the corvée for canal-clearance still an annual obligation. The Nilometer of Roda, rebuilt in 861, was the system's control instrument, and the whole apparatus of survey, gauging and criers turned the river's behaviour directly into the year's tax revenue.
entries.note: Karl Butzer, Early Hydraulic Civilization in Egypt (1976) for the basin system's long continuity; William Willcocks, Egyptian Irrigation (1899) on the technique. Canal corvée: the papyri and Frantz-Murphy (1986).

entries.label: The Egyptian congregational mosque
entries.hint: The mosque became the defining building type. Egyptian builders developed the hypostyle plan — a broad columned prayer hall opening onto an arcaded courtyard — using brick, re-used ancient columns, and imported ideas: the Ibn Tulun mosque's brick piers, pointed arches, carved stucco friezes and spiral minaret came from the caliphal capital of Samarra. Over two centuries the form spread from the mosque of 'Amr to every town, carrying with it new techniques of vaulting, plasterwork and joinery.
entries.note: K.A.C. Creswell, Early Muslim Architecture (1932–40) vols.1–2. Doris Behrens-Abouseif, Islamic Architecture in Cairo: An Introduction (1989).

entries.label: Lustre, tin-glaze and the figured loom
entries.hint: Egypt was a transfer point for three demanding craft technologies of the age. Tin-opacified white glaze gave potters a ceramic 'canvas'; lustre painting — a copper-and-silver film fired in a reducing atmosphere to leave a metallic sheen — was a genuine chemical innovation shared between Iraq and Egypt; and the drawloom let weavers produce the complex repeated patterns and inscription bands of tiraz silk. Egyptian workshops adopted, refined and re-exported all three.
entries.note: Oliver Watson, Ceramics from Islamic Lands (2004); Marilyn Jenkins-Madina on the lustre question. The drawloom: R.B. Serjeant, Islamic Textiles (1972).

entries.label: The war fleet and the dockyards
entries.hint: Egypt's shipyards (dar al-sina'a), on Roda island and at the Delta ports, built the galleys that won the Battle of the Masts in 655 and made the province the caliphate's Mediterranean naval power. The fleet declined under the later Abbasids, was rebuilt by Ibn Tulun, and mattered again to the Ikhshidids facing the Fatimids by sea. Naval technology — the war galley, the fire-ship, the transport — was one field where Egypt stayed continuously capable.
entries.note: Ekkehard Eickhoff, Seekrieg und Seepolitik zwischen Islam und Abendland (1966); Aly Mohamed Fahmy, Muslim Sea-Power in the Eastern Mediterranean (1950). The Roda dockyard: al-Maqrizi, Khitat.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Arab settlement and slow conversion, the Nubian baqt treaty, and Fustat as a Mediterranean entrepot

entries.label: Arab settlement and the long shift
entries.hint: The conquest brought a garrison; over the following centuries came further Arab migration and the drift of Bedouin groups into Middle and Upper Egypt, mixing with the population. Arabisation of language and Islamisation of faith were slow, uneven, and mostly still ahead in 969 — Coptic was still spoken in the villages and Christians were still a majority — but the mechanisms were all in place: intermarriage, the tax incentive, the ceiling on non-Muslim advancement, and the prestige of the rulers' language and religion.
entries.note: Richard Bulliet, Conversion to Islam in the Medieval Period (1979); Tamer el-Leithy, 'Coptic Culture and Conversion in Medieval Cairo, 1293–1524' (2005) for the later acceleration. Petra Sijpesteijn, Shaping a Muslim State (2013).

entries.label: The baqt with Christian Nubia
entries.hint: After a failed invasion in 652, Egypt and the Christian kingdom of Makuria settled into a unique arrangement, the baqt: not a tribute but a reciprocal annual exchange — Nubia delivering a fixed number of slaves and some ivory and cattle, Egypt sending wheat, lentils, cloth, wine and horses — together with mutual security guarantees and rights for traders and travellers. It held, with interruptions, for six centuries, the longest-lasting treaty between an Islamic state and a Christian one.
entries.note: Giovanni Vantini, Oriental Sources concerning Nubia (1975); Jay Spaulding, 'Medieval Christian Nubia and the Islamic World: A Reconsideration of the Baqt Treaty', International Journal of African Historical Studies 28 (1995). Derek Welsby, The Medieval Kingdoms of Nubia (2002).

entries.label: Fustat, the hinge of three seas
entries.hint: Fustat sat where the Nile met the routes to the Mediterranean (through Alexandria, Damietta and Tinnis) and to the Red Sea (through Qulzum, and later the caravan from Qus to 'Aydhab). Goods crossed it in every direction — Sudanese gold and slaves, Indian pepper and spices, Baltic amber and Frankish swords, Egyptian linen and grain, timber and iron. The trader Ibn Khordadbeh, writing around 850, describes Jewish 'Radhanite' merchants running a circuit from Francia to China that passed through Egypt each way.
entries.note: Ibn Khordadbeh, Kitab al-Masalik wa-al-Mamalik (the Radhanite passage). S.D. Goitein, A Mediterranean Society (1967–93), for the fuller Geniza-era picture rooted in this period; Moshe Gil, 'The Radhanite Merchants and the Land of Radhan', JESHO 17 (1974).

entries.label: The canal, Qulzum and the Red Sea revival
entries.hint: 'Amr re-dug the Nile–Red Sea canal to ship Egyptian grain to the Hijaz — the 'Canal of the Commander of the Faithful', kept open for over a century until a caliph ordered it filled to blockade a rebel Medina around 770. The port of Qulzum at its Red Sea end, and the trade of Yemen, East Africa and India, kept the route alive, and as Baghdad and the Persian Gulf declined in the tenth century the Indian Ocean spice trade began the shift toward the Red Sea and Egypt that the Fatimids would complete.
entries.note: John Cooper, The Medieval Nile: Route, Navigation, and Landscape in Islamic Egypt (2014). The canal: al-Maqrizi, Khitat; al-Baladhuri. Red Sea trade: Timothy Power, The Red Sea from Byzantium to the Caliphate (2012).
keywords: Canal of the Commander of the Faithful

entries.label: Sea war, truces and the Cretan emirate
entries.hint: Egypt and Byzantium fought a long, low-level war of raid and counter-raid across the eastern Mediterranean, punctuated by truces and formal exchanges of prisoners on the frontier. Trade never entirely stopped — Byzantine gold and Egyptian linen and papyrus still crossed. A striking offshoot: a band of Andalusi Muslims expelled from Alexandria in the 820s went on to conquer Crete and found an emirate that raided the Aegean for over a century, until Byzantium retook the island in 961.
entries.note: The Cretan emirate: Vassilios Christides, The Conquest of Crete by the Arabs (1984). Sea war: Eickhoff, Seekrieg und Seepolitik (1966). Prisoner exchanges: the Byzantine–Arab literature on the fida'.

entries.label: The Fatimid da'wa reaches Egypt
entries.hint: Long before Jawhar's army, the Isma'ili Shiʿi missionary network (da'wa) of the Fatimid caliphs of North Africa was active in Egypt, winning converts and gathering intelligence among a population disillusioned with Abbasid neglect. The conquest of 969 completed a reorientation: Egypt, which had spent three centuries as an eastern province looking to Baghdad, became the heart of a Mediterranean empire whose other pole was Ifriqiya, and whose court brought a whole new religious and intellectual culture with it.
entries.note: Michael Brett, The Rise of the Fatimids (2001) and The Fatimid Empire (2017); Heinz Halm, The Empire of the Mahdi (1996). The da'wa in Egypt: Yaacov Lev, 'The Fatimids and Egypt 301–358/914–969', Studia Islamica 66 (1987).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: Fustat the new metropolis, the Nile and its failing floods, and the Nubian kingdoms to the south

entries.label: Fustat, the new metropolis
entries.hint: From a tribal camp Fustat grew into one of the largest cities in the world — several hundred thousand people by the tenth century, the biggest west of Baghdad. Travellers describe tall apartment blocks of several storeys housing hundreds, a piped water and drainage system, sprawling markets, the smoking potters' and dyers' quarters, distinct Christian and Jewish neighbourhoods, and the vast tomb-city of the Qarafa spreading into the desert. Cairo, founded next door in 969, would eventually absorb it.
entries.note: Al-Muqaddasi, Ahsan al-Taqasim (10th c.); Nasir-i Khusraw, Safarnama (11th c., but describing the mature city). Wladimir Kubiak, Al-Fustat (1987); the excavation reports of Scanlon and Gayraud.

entries.label: The Nile and the failing floods
entries.hint: The graduated column of the Roda Nilometer recorded, year on year, the height on which everything depended, and the tenth century brought a run of bad ones. Low or failed floods and famine struck repeatedly, worst in 967–968, when grain prices soared, people died in the streets of Fustat, and the Ikhshidid treasury could not cope. The dynasty's collapse and the Fatimid takeover happened in the middle of a subsistence crisis that the river had caused.
entries.note: William Popper, The Cairo Nilometer (1951) — the reading series. Famine chronology: al-Maqrizi, Ighathat al-umma bi-kashf al-ghumma (his history of Egyptian famines); Michael Brett, The Rise of the Fatimids (2001) pp.295–314.

entries.label: The Christian kingdoms of Nubia at their height
entries.hint: South of the cataract, the kingdom of Makuria — which had absorbed Nobadia — and, further up, Alodia were prosperous Christian states in their golden age. Old Dongola had a domed audience hall, a stone-built cathedral and painted churches; the kingdoms took their bishops from the Coptic patriarch, traded across the baqt frontier, and were strong enough that a Nubian king could march an army into Egypt to protest the mistreatment of the church. Egypt never seriously tried to conquer them.
entries.note: Derek Welsby, The Medieval Kingdoms of Nubia (2002); Włodzimierz Godlewski, Dongola: Ancient Tungul (2013). The Nubian intervention of 745 (over the imprisoned patriarch Khaʾil I): the History of the Patriarchs.

entries.label: The deserts, the Beja and the gold
entries.hint: The deserts framed Islamic Egypt as raiding frontier and resource. The Western oases dwindled into places of exile; Bedouin groups drifted into the valley; and in the southeast the Beja, the desert people between the Nile and the Red Sea, both raided Upper Egypt and controlled the approaches to the gold. Abbasid treaties in 831 and 854 opened the Wadi Allaqi goldfields to Egyptian and Arab miners, and a rough boom town grew there before the veins gave out.
entries.note: Al-Ya'qubi, al-Buldan; al-Maqrizi on the Beja treaties. The Allaqi mining settlement: the survey work of the Eastern Desert projects; Timothy Power, The Red Sea from Byzantium to the Caliphate (2012).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The governor Qurra ibn Sharik, the jurist al-Shafiʿi, the eunuch Kafur, and the villagers of the papyri

entries.label: Basileios of Aphrodito, the last Christian pagarch
entries.hint: Basileios ran the district of Aphrodito as its pagarch under the Umayyad governor Qurra ibn Sharik. His archive — hundreds of documents in Greek, Coptic and Arabic — shows a Christian official caught between an Egyptian village and an increasingly demanding Muslim state: collecting the tax silver and the wheat, drafting the labour and the sailors, chasing the runaways, and forwarding polite, anxious letters to a governor who threatened him with punishment for every shortfall. He is the best-documented individual of the whole century.
entries.note: The subject of Petra Sijpesteijn, Shaping a Muslim State: The World of a Mid-Eighth-Century Egyptian Official (2013), built around his archive; the texts in Bell, Greek Papyri in the British Museum IV (1910) and the Coptic and Arabic corpora.

entries.label: al-Shafiʿi's Egyptian years
entries.hint: Al-Shafiʿi came to Fustat in his late forties, disillusioned with Baghdad, and spent his last six years teaching a circle in the mosque of 'Amr and dictating the works of his maturity to disciples — al-Buwayti, al-Muzani, al-Rabiʿ ibn Sulayman — who carried his teaching forward. He revised positions he had held for decades in the light of Egyptian debate and evidence. He died in 820 and was buried in the Qarafa; the jurisprudence he finished there became the law of Egypt.
entries.note: The biographical tradition (Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bayhaqi's Manaqib al-Shafiʿi). Joseph Lowry, Early Islamic Legal Theory (2007); Ahmed El Shamsy, The Canonisation of Islamic Law (2013).

entries.label: Ahmad ibn Tulun
entries.hint: Ibn Tulun was a hard, pious, tireless man — a memoriser of the Qurʾan and a student of hadith who rose from the son of a Turkish slave-soldier to the founder of a state. He built ceaselessly, endowed a free hospital, and could be savage: after the Tarsus garrison defied him he is said to have had many of them killed. His last years were soured by his son al-Abbas's revolt and by illness. He left Egypt richer and stronger than it had been in a thousand years, and a son who lost it all.
entries.note: Al-Balawi, Sirat Ahmad ibn Tulun; Ibn al-Daya. Zaky M. Hassan, Les Tulunides (1933); Thierry Bianquis in CHE1 (1998).

entries.label: Kafur, the slave who ruled Egypt
entries.hint: Bought as a boy, castrated, and given to al-Ikhshid, Kafur rose by sheer competence to command the army, then to run the state as regent, then — with the caliph's title and his name in the Friday prayer — to rule it outright. Contemporaries could not get past the fact of a black eunuch slave governing Egypt: al-Mutanabbi's poems about him are as cruel as they are brilliant. But his government was careful and effective, he kept the country whole against real dangers, and he was buried, as he wished, near Jerusalem.
entries.note: Al-Mutanabbi, Diwan; Ibn Khallikan, Wafayat al-A'yan; al-Maqrizi. Jere Bacharach, 'African Military Slaves in the Medieval Middle East', IJMES 13 (1981).

entries.label: Severus ibn al-Muqaffa'
entries.hint: Severus began as a government secretary, became a monk after a crisis of conscience, and was made bishop of al-Ashmunayn. He was the intellectual leader of a Coptic church learning to defend itself in Arabic: he debated Muslim and Jewish scholars at the vizier's request, wrote accessible Arabic theology for a community losing its Coptic, and set in motion the History of the Patriarchs. His career is a portrait of how a minority keeps its identity while adopting its rulers' language.
entries.note: Severus's works: the collected editions of R.Y. Ebied, L.R. Wickham and others; Samir Khalil Samir on the Christian Arabic corpus. Sidney Griffith, The Church in the Shadow of the Mosque (2008).

entries.label: The villagers and traders of the papyri
entries.hint: Beneath the governors and jurists, the Arabic and Coptic papyri and the oldest Geniza fragments preserve ordinary lives: a peasant petitioning against an over-assessment, a flax-worker's wage dispute, a small merchant's consignment note, a woman's marriage settlement and her later divorce, a letter chasing a runaway servant or a debt, a monastery's account of its harvest. Together they document, village by village and household by household, what the coming of Islam actually meant on the ground — and how gradual it was.
entries.note: The Arabic papyrology of Adolf Grohmann and the Vienna, Michigan and Cambridge collections; the Coptic documentary texts. Petra Sijpesteijn & Lennart Sundelin (eds.), Papyrology and the History of Early Islamic Egypt (2004).
